messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 57
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Tutor
- Trauma Type: Sexual assault
- Pcl5: 66

# The Weight of What Was Done

Marcus is a 57-year-old man who works as a private tutor, spending his days helping high school students navigate calculus and chemistry in the quiet of their family dining rooms. He is soft-spoken, methodical, and precise — qualities that have served him well in his profession and that he has, over the years, learned to wear like armor.

Three years ago, Marcus was sexually assaulted by an acquaintance he had known through a community choir. The man had invited him back to his apartment after a rehearsal, and what Marcus had understood to be a friendly evening became something he still cannot fully bring himself to name aloud. He did not report it. He told himself, in the weeks that followed, that he wasn't sure anyone would believe him — that men his age, men in general, weren't supposed to need that kind of help. He drove home that night in a state he describes only as "somewhere else," and he has never quite found his way back.

In the months after the assault, Marcus began reorganizing his life around avoidance. He quit the choir without explanation. He stopped attending the small dinner parties that had once punctuated his otherwise solitary routine. He changed his jogging route so that it would not take him past the street where the man lived. Each of these changes felt, at the time, like reasonable precautions. Together, they quietly hollowed out the life he had built.

Sleep became its own ordeal. Marcus wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, his heart hammering, the sheets damp. The dreams are not always explicit — sometimes they are only a feeling, a weight, a locked door — but he wakes from them the same way every time: certain that something is still happening to him. During the day, he moves through a low-grade hypervigilance that exhausts him. He sits with his back to the wall at coffee shops. He notices exits. When a student's father comes to the door unexpectedly, his body floods with adrenaline before his mind can catch up.

What troubles Marcus most, and what he speaks about with the most difficulty, is what the assault has done to his sense of himself. He had always understood himself to be a careful, self-possessed man. He had been single for many years by choice, or so he had believed, and he had found genuine meaning in his independence. Now he wonders, with a corrosive persistence, whether he had somehow invited what happened — whether something about him had communicated vulnerability, or willingness, or weakness. He knows, intellectually, that this is not true. Knowing has not helped.

His work as a tutor has become both a refuge and a source of quiet grief. The structure of a tutoring session — the problem, the method, the solution — offers him something reliable in days that otherwise feel shapeless. He is good at it, and his students trust him. But there are moments, sitting across a kitchen table from a teenager, when he is struck by a sudden, vertiginous sense of unreality, as though he is watching himself from a distance. He loses the thread of what he was explaining. He excuses himself to the bathroom and stands at the sink until the feeling passes.

Marcus has not told anyone what happened to him. Not a friend, not a sibling, not a doctor. He carries it the way he has learned to carry most difficult things — alone, efficiently, with the quiet competence of a man who has always believed that managing one's own pain is simply part of being an adult. He is beginning to suspect, with something that feels almost like relief, that this particular belief may have cost him more than he realized.
